questions.q: What was the primary institutional innovation of the Anand-pattern dairy cooperative that distinguished it from government-run dairy schemes?
questions.a: The Anand-pattern made milk producers (farmers) the owners and governors of the cooperative through elected village societies, district unions, and a state federation — eliminating government bureaucrats from daily management. A wrong answer like "it used pasteurization technology" or "it gave subsidies to farmers" reveals confusion between technical inputs and institutional ownership structure.

questions.q: Explain why Operation Flood was implemented in phases (Phase I: 1970-80, Phase II: 1981-85, Phase III: 1985-96) rather than as a single nationwide rollout.
questions.a: Phasing allowed learning from early regions (Gujarat, Maharashtra) to refine the cooperative model, build management capacity, and establish milk-shed linkages before expanding to less developed areas. A wrong answer like "due to budget constraints" misses the deliberate institutional learning design — Phase I created 18 milk sheds, Phase II added 136, Phase III consolidated 73,000 village societies.

questions.q: A village in eastern Uttar Pradesh has 200 households: 40 landless Dalit families (1 buffalo each), 100 OBC small farmers (2 buffaloes each), 50 upper-caste medium farmers (5 buffaloes each), and 10 large farmers (20 buffaloes each). If a dairy cooperative is formed with one-member-one-vote, which group would likely dominate the managing committee and why?
questions.a: Upper-caste medium farmers would likely dominate because they have higher milk surplus (more marketable surplus), greater literacy, existing social networks, and historical dominance in local institutions — despite one-member-one-vote. A wrong answer assuming "landless families would control it because they are more numerous" ignores how social capital and resource control translate into cooperative leadership.

questions.q: Compare the Green Revolution and White Revolution on: (a) primary resource required, (b) scale of farmer benefited, (c) impact on women's labour, (d) regional spread.
questions.a: (a) Green Revolution: irrigation + HYV seeds + chemicals; White Revolution: milch animal + fodder + veterinary care. (b) Green Revolution benefited medium/large farmers with irrigated land; White Revolution reached landless/marginal farmers with 1-2 animals. (c) Green Revolution displaced women from processing (mechanization); White Revolution increased women's dairy work (feeding, milking) but often without control over income. (d) Green Revolution concentrated in Punjab/Haryana/western UP; White Revolution spread to 170+ milk sheds across 22 states. A wrong answer claiming "both benefited small farmers equally" misses the land vs. livestock asset distinction.

questions.q: Critique the statement: "Operation Flood succeeded because it bypassed caste hierarchies by organizing purely on economic interest."
questions.a: The statement is false. Cooperatives often replicated caste hierarchies: dominant castes (Patels in Gujarat, Marathas in Maharashtra) controlled leadership; Dalits were excluded from management or received lower prices citing "quality"; women's labour was exploited while men held membership. Success came from aligning with, not bypassing, local power structures. A wrong answer accepting the statement ignores sociological evidence that cooperatives are embedded in, not external to, agrarian social relations.

questions.q: Design a dairy cooperative model for a tribal region in Jharkhand where: (i) households own 1-2 goats not cows/buffaloes, (ii) no all-weather roads, (iii) women do all animal care but men handle cash, (iv) nearest town is 40km. Specify: membership rules, collection logistics, governance safeguards for women, and one innovation to prevent elite capture.
questions.a: Good answer: (1) Membership per animal (not per household) so women goat-keepers join directly. (2) Cluster-based collection: women's self-help groups collect at hamlet level, use insulated cans on bicycles to chilling centre at block HQ. (3) 50% women in managing committee; separate women's general body; milk payment directly to women's bank accounts. (4) Innovation: rotating chairmanship by hamlet + social audit by Gram Sabha. Poor answer copies Anand model without adapting to goat milk, terrain, gender norms, or tribal social structure.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The White Revolution (Operation Flood) was a national dairy development programme launched in 1970 by the National Dairy Development Board (NDDB) to create a nationwide milk grid, increase milk production through ______ structures, and ensure fair prices for smallholder milk producers by eliminating middlemen.
Fill in the blank: Imagine a ______ Dalit woman in 1970s Gujarat who owns one buffalo but sells milk to a local trader at ₹2/litre while he sells it in the city for ₹6.

Fill in the blank: The White Revolution (Operation Flood) was a national dairy development programme launched in ______ by the National Dairy Development Board (NDDB) to create a nationwide milk grid, increase milk production through cooperative structures, and ensure fair prices for smallholder milk producers by eliminating middlemen.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain the three-phase structure of Operation Flood, describe the Anand-pattern cooperative model (village society → district union → state federation), and analyze its differential impact on landless households, women, and dominant castes across regions.
